title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate the ability to calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state their answers clearly. For 2.5 Equations, students should be able to calculate solutions to linear and quadratic equations, show that their solutions are correct, and explain their methods. When solving simultaneous equations, students should be able to justify their choice of method and state their answers clearly. Working should be shown for all calculations, especially when using the quadratic formula or completing the square.
### Traps
Common mistakes include forgetting to multiply through by the LCD when working with fractions, adding instead of subtracting when eliminating variables in simultaneous equations, and not verifying answers by substituting them back into the original equation. Another trap is not defining the unknown clearly in word problems, leading to incorrect equations.
### Memory hooks
To make this topic easier to remember, students can use the mnemonic 'LCD' to recall the steps for solving linear equations with fractions. They can also use the pattern of 'add, subtract, multiply, divide' to remember the order of operations when solving simultaneous equations. A shortcut for completing the square is to remember that the constant term is always -(b/2)^2 + c. Students can also sanity-check their answers by graphing the related functions or using a calculator to verify their solutions.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total exam time. Students should budget around 20-30 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the difficulty and complexity of the questions. It is essential to read the questions carefully and allocate time accordingly to ensure that all parts of the question are answered.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate their ability to design and problem-solve using algorithms, as stated in statement 7. For calculate questions, show working and justify answers. For explain and describe questions, provide clear and concise pseudocode or flowcharts. For justify and state questions, provide a reason or explanation for the answer. 
### Traps
Common mistakes include not using ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators in pseudocode, not recording condition results in trace tables, and not testing boundary values. Correction: always use terminators, record condition results, and test boundary values. 
### Memory hooks
To remember the difference between validation and verification, use the mnemonic 'valid' for checking data format and 'verify' for checking data accuracy. To remember the linear search algorithm, think of 'looking for a book on a shelf'. To sanity-check an answer, test it with a simple example. 
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer the questions. Make sure to read the questions carefully and manage time effectively to earn the maximum marks.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Exam technique: Data Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on number systems (1.1), show full working in conversions, e.g. binary to decimal to hex. For text, sound and images (1.2), explain how character sets and colour depth affect file size. For data storage and compression (1.3), justify the use of lossless or lossy compression. Command words like calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used, with working and reasons required for full marks.
### Traps
Error: incorrect conversion between number systems. Correction: double-check place values and use the correct conversion method. Error: forgetting to include metadata in file size calculations. Correction: remember to include width, height, and depth in bitmap image calculations. Error: using lossy compression for text files. Correction: use lossless compression for text files to preserve exact data.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic BIC (Binary, Integer, Character) to remember the different number systems. For binary to decimal conversion, use the pattern of doubling the previous place value. To sanity-check file size calculations, use the formula: file size (bits) = W x H x depth. Write down the conversion method before starting a question to ensure accuracy.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, with 2-3 questions. Budget around 30-40 minutes to answer these questions, depending on the complexity and your familiarity with the topic.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²

Exam tips: never mix degrees into s = rθ; convert first. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing, and check whether a question asks for the major or minor sector.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 2.1, explain why serial transmission is reliable over distance and describe the benefits of packet switching, including robustness and shared lines. For 2.2, state the purpose of checksums and explain how they detect errors. For 2.3, describe the process of encryption and justify its importance in secure data transmission. For 3.4, describe the functions of network hardware components, including routers, switches, and gateways.
### Traps
Error: confusing MAC and IP addresses. Correction: MAC addresses are burned-in and used for layer 2 communication, while IP addresses are assigned and used for layer 3 communication. Error: assuming parallel transmission is always faster. Correction: parallel transmission is faster over short distances, but serial transmission is more reliable over long distances. Error: thinking that HTTPS is a protocol. Correction: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, a secure protocol for data transmission.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' to remember the layers of the TCP/IP stack: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application. To compare MAC and IP addresses, use a table to highlight their differences. To remember the functions of network hardware components, associate each component with its function, such as routers 'routing' traffic between networks.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on networking and communication. Make sure to allocate time to read the questions carefully and plan your answers before starting to write.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function)
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential)

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

title: Probability and Statistics I
content:
Probability and Statistics I

Permutations and Combinations

  • Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!
  • Combinations (order irrelevant): ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Example: choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: C(8,3) = 56. Arranging 3 of 8 books on a shelf: P(8,3) = 336.

Probability Rules

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
  • Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
  • Complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Tree diagrams multiply along branches and add across outcomes.

Example: P(two reds without replacement from 5 red + 3 blue) = (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14.

Discrete Random Variables

E(X) = Σ x P(X = x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

Example: die: E(X) = 3.5; E(X²) = 91/6, so Var(X) ≈ 2.92.

Exam tips: decide permutation vs combination by testing whether swapping two items changes the outcome; always verify tree-branch probabilities sum to 1.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The Nucleus

Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Nuclear densities are enormous (~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) — nearly all mass in a tiny volume.

Radioactive Decay

Random and spontaneous:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A samemm of aluminium
gammanothingthick lead

Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay. N = N₀ e^(−λt), λ = ln 2 / t½.

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days: after 30 days, 1/8 of the original activity remains.

Mass–Energy

E = mc². Mass difference Δm in nuclear reactions becomes energy; binding energy = energy released assembling the nucleus. 1 u ≈ 931 MeV.

Fission and Fusion

Both release energy by moving toward iron (peak binding energy per nucleon): heavy nuclei split (fission, reactors), light nuclei merge (fusion, stars).

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every equation; activity questions use A = λN, not guesswork with halves.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to precisely name the threat and provide the matched defence. For example, when asked to explain a security threat, students should state the threat, such as pharming, and then describe the defence, such as keeping DNS servers and hosts files secure and checking HTTPS certificates. Command words like explain, describe, and justify are commonly used in this topic's questions. Students should also be able to apply ethical principles to scenarios, as outlined in the ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes, and show how they affect stakeholders and consequences.
### Traps
A common mistake is confusing phishing and pharming. Another error is not providing a matched defence for a given threat. Students should also avoid giving opinions instead of principle-based answers in ethics questions.
### Memory hooks
To remember the types of malware, students can use the mnemonic VIRUS: V for virus, I for intercept, R for ransomware, U for unsecured, and S for spyware. Another hook is to associate each type of threat with its corresponding defence. For example, malware is defended against with anti-malware software. Students can also use a diagram to illustrate the blockchain concept and its components.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the paper, and students should budget around 10-12 minutes to answer the questions. Students should allocate their time according to the marks available for each question and make sure to read the questions carefully to avoid common traps.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate a clear understanding of the concepts. For 3.1, explain the von Neumann model and the FDE cycle, showing how instructions are stored as data. For 3.2, describe input and output devices, and for 3.3, compare different storage types, justifying their use cases. Command words like explain, describe, and justify require working and a reason to be shown.
### Traps
Common mistakes include confusing the roles of the PC and MAR registers, and not understanding the difference between RAM and ROM. Another error is not considering the effects of performance factors like clock speed and cache size. Correction: review the FDE cycle and the characteristics of each storage type.
### Memory hooks
To remember the FDE cycle, use the mnemonic Fetch-Decode-Execute. For the types of buses, think address-data-control. To compare storage types, consider the acronym CAPD: capacity, access time, portability, and durability. Finally, to sanity-check an answer, ask whether it aligns with the stored program concept.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, so budget around 30-40 minutes for it. Make sure to leave time to review and check your work.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For 1.1 Data Representation, calculate earns marks for correct binary arithmetic and two's complement conversions, showing working. Explain earns marks for describing number systems and their ranges. For 1.2 Multimedia Graphics, describe earns marks for outlining bitmap and sound representation. For 1.3 Compression, justify earns marks for stating why a compression type suits the data, with reasons.
### Traps
Error: incorrect two's complement conversion, Correction: remember the MSB has value -2^(n-1). Error: confusing lossless and lossy compression, Correction: lossless is required for text and code. Error: incorrect calculation of file size, Correction: check the formula, e.g. width x height x depth for bitmap images.
### Memory hooks
To remember binary arithmetic rules, use the mnemonic '0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1'. For two's complement, recall 'invert and add 1'. To check the number of bits required for a number, use the formula 2^n - 1. For compression, associate lossless with text and lossy with images and sound.
### Timing
Information Representation is around 20-25% of the paper, budget 30-40 minutes for these questions.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹).

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 5.1 and 5.2 questions, explain and describe the structure and function of web technologies, including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Use command words like explain, describe, and state to earn marks. For example, explaining how the DOM is used to add interactivity to a web page can earn full marks. Justify and show that commands may require working or a reason to be shown.
### Traps
Error: writing HTML tags without correct closing pairs. Correction: always write tags with correct closing pairs. Error: not separating structure, presentation, and behaviour in answers. Correction: separate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in answers. Error: not explaining DOM operations correctly. Correction: explain DOM operations as 'find element by id ... then change property'.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'HTML is the structure, CSS is the style, and JavaScript is the action' to remember the separation of web technologies. To sanity-check an answer, ask yourself 'is this a structure, presentation, or behaviour question?'. Write down the layers of a web page (structure, presentation, behaviour) before starting an answer.
### Timing
Budget around 30-40 minutes for this topic's share of the paper. This topic usually accounts for 2-3 questions, each worth around 10-15 marks.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: Deformation

Hooke's Law

Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Springs in series share the load (k_total < each); in parallel, k_total adds.

Stress, Strain, Young Modulus

  • Stress σ = F/A (Pa)
  • Strain ε = x/L (no unit)
  • Young modulus E = σ/ε (Pa) — a material property, independent of shape

Example: a wire of length 2 m, cross-section 1 × 10⁻⁶ m², extends 1 mm under 100 N: E = (F/A)/(x/L) = (10⁸)/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa — steel-like.

Force–Extension Graphs

  • Gradient of the linear region = k
  • Area under graph = elastic PE stored = ½Fx (for linear) = ½kx²
  • Beyond the yield point the wire deforms plastically and will not return

Breaking Stress

The maximum stress a material withstands — strong materials have high breaking stress, stiff materials have high E.

Exam tips: convert mm to m and mm² to m² before substituting; the area under a stress–strain graph gives energy per unit volume.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and Equilibrium

Free-Body Diagrams

Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Resolving Forces

Any force F at angle θ splits into F cos θ (along) and F sin θ (perpendicular).

Example: a 50 N pull at 30° above horizontal drags with 50 cos 30° ≈ 43.3 N horizontally.

An object on a slope of angle θ has components mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into it.

Equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force is zero in every direction and the resultant moment is zero.

Moments and the Principle of Moments

Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.

For equilibrium: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments.

Example: a 600 N child 2 m from a pivot balances an adult 1.2 m away: 600 × 2 = W × 1.2, so W = 1000 N.

Centre of Gravity

The point where the weight appears to act. For stable equilibrium the line of action must pass through the base.

Exam tips: take moments about the point with the most unknown forces; include the normal reaction and friction of any support, and check units of perpendicular distance.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.
