title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Force on a Current

F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Example: 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A at 90° to a 0.2 T field: F = 0.3 N.

Force on a Moving Charge

F = BQv sin θ, always perpendicular to v → circular paths: r = mv/(BQ) (basis of cyclotrons and mass spectrometers).

Example: an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in 0.5 mT: r ≈ 2.3 cm.

Fields from Currents

  • Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr), circling by the right-hand grip rule
  • Solenoid: B = μ₀nI inside

Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday: induced EMF = rate of flux cutting = N dΦ/dt. Lenz: induced effects oppose the change (negative sign).

Example: a coil of 100 turns, flux changing 2 mWb in 50 ms induces EMF = 100 × 0.002/0.05 = 4 V.

Flux Φ = BA (B ⊥ A). Generators rotate coils in fields; transformers link two coils by a shared changing flux with V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂.

Exam tips: use left hand for motors (force on current), right hand for generators (induced current); state Lenz's law in explain questions.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Probability and Statistics II
content:
Probability and Statistics II

Normal Distribution

Continuous, bell-shaped, defined by mean μ and variance σ². Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).

Example: X ~ N(50, 4²). P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards problems: given a probability, find μ or σ from the z-value: x = μ + zσ.

Binomial Distribution

Fixed n independent trials, success probability p: P(X = r) = C(n, r) pʳ (1−p)^(n−r). Mean np, variance np(1 − p).

Example: n = 5, p = 0.2: P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.04 × 0.8³ = 0.2048.

Normal Approximation to Binomial

Valid when np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: P(X ≤ 10) becomes P(Y < 10.5) under Y ~ N(np, np(1−p)).

Expectation and Variance Rules

E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). For sums: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).

Exam tips: always sketch the normal curve and shade the region; state the distribution you are using; never forget the continuity correction when approximating a discrete variable.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Internal Energy

Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Specific Heat and Latent Heat

  • Heating: Q = mcΔθ (c = specific heat capacity)
  • Phase change: Q = mL (L = specific latent heat)

Example: melting 0.2 kg ice: Q = 0.2 × 334,000 ≈ 67 kJ — no temperature change during the change.

Mixtures: heat lost = heat gained.

Gas Laws

  • Boyle: pV = constant (T fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant (p fixed)
  • Pressure law: p/T = constant (V fixed)
  • Combined/ideal: pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Example: 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³: p = nRT/V = 2 × 8.31 × 300/0.05 ≈ 100 kPa.

Kinetic Theory

½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT — temperature measures mean translational KE. Also pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.

Exam tips: use kelvin in every gas equation; in mixture problems, work per substance with a common final temperature.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

title: Exam technique: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks, ensure you understand the command words: calculate for truth tables, show that for circuit construction, explain and describe for logic expressions. Justify and state are used for problem-to-logic mapping, where defining inputs and outputs earns marks. See statement 10.
### Traps
Error: incorrect truth table row count. Correction: check the number of inputs to determine the row count. Error: writing NOT before a gate. Correction: NOT inverts the output, not the input. Error: incorrect order of operations in logic expressions. Correction: brackets first, then AND, then OR.
### Memory hooks
To remember the six gates, use the mnemonic AND, OR, and NOT to create the others. For truth tables, use the pattern 2 inputs = 4 rows, 3 inputs = 8 rows. To sanity-check a logic expression, plug in values from the truth table.
### Timing
This topic accounts for approximately 10% of the paper. Budget 10-15 minutes to answer questions on logic gates and Boolean logic.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Circular Motion

Angular speed ω = v/r = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹). Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r, always directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string at 2 m s⁻¹ needs F = 2 N inward.

Gravitational Field

Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

Field strength g = GM/r². At Earth's surface g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Orbits

For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) — higher orbits move slower but have longer periods (Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³).

Geostationary satellites: T = 24 h, r ≈ 42,300 km from the centre.

Potential

Gravitational potential φ = −GM/r (zero at infinity). Potential gradient gives field strength: g = −dφ/dr.

Exam tips: speed in orbit is independent of the satellite's own mass; don't confuse g at the surface with orbital equations using r from the planet's centre.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.
